Stated Claim / Post Context:
Plagued by knots, frizz and frazzled ends? Blow-dry your hair from the bottom up, expert says

According toAnabel Kingsley, brand president and lead consultant at Philip Kingsley, many of us have been blow-drying our hair in completely the wrong order.

Actual Article Body:
By XANTHA LEATHAM, EXECUTIVE SCIENCE EDITOR

Published:  21:41 AEST, 27 September 2026   |  Updated:  23:41 AEST, 27 September 2026

When you’re having a bad hair day it can feel like knots, frizz and split ends are impossible to control.

But it turns out that there is an easy way to turn this situation on its head – and it’s because many of us are blow-drying our hair in completely the wrong order.

Most people start at their roots and work down, but one hair expert believes a smarter approach is to begin with the lengths and ends before moving up.

Anabel Kingsley, brand president and lead consultant at haircare brand Philip Kingsley, told the Daily Mail: 'If you dry the top of your hair first, your lengths can be blown about in different directions.

'As the ends of hair are generally wispier, as well as more damaged and more porous, it leaves them prone to sticking and tangling together, especially when they are damp.

'Apart from leaving your ends looking frazzled, this can lead to breakage.'

Experts say we should be blow-drying our hair from the bottom up to prevent knots and frizz

In her new book, called Haircare: The Ultimate Guide, Ms Kingsley explains that if you start drying hair at the top or front, tangles and frizz will form throughout your ends.

A lot of this comes down to the way hydrogen bonds behave inside the hair.

'Hydrogen bonds are your hair's weakest but most numerous bonds,' Ms Kingsley explained. 'They break when you wet your hair and reset when your hair dries.'

These bonds allow people to style their hair into different shapes.

They are also affected by humidity in the atmosphere, which is why carefully styled hair can quickly lose its shape on a damp or rainy day.

Ms Kingsley explained that drying the top section first causes hydrogen bonds in the lengths to reset randomly, leaving hair looking frizzy and dry.

As a result, many people reach for higher temperatures or more aggressive styling techniques in an attempt to smooth everything back down.

But this could be doing more harm than good.

'Your ends, being older, are already more porous and weathered, so you really want to treat them gently,' Ms Kingsley said.

Instead, the expert recommends drying the ends while they are still damp, rather than soaking wet, using low to medium heat.

This makes it easier to shape the hair without relying on excessive heat or tension from a brush.

Meanwhile, the roots typically take much longer to dry because hair is denser at the scalp.

By the time the ends have been styled, the roots should still be damp enough to manipulate into shape.

And if they aren't, Ms Kingsley suggests lightly misting them with water rather than turning the heat setting up higher.

'Of course, everyone's hair is different and some people may find they like the results of drying the top of their hair first – but I encourage you to give my method a go as it works very well for our clinic clients,' she said.

Haircare: The Ultimate Guide by Anabel Kingsley (Piatkus, £25) is available here.
